item.title: It’s finally farm bill week
item.content:encoded:
Presented by Bayer: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by Bayer

With help from Grace Yarrow and Meredith Lee Hill

House Agriculture Chair Glenn Thompson (R-Pa.) at the Capitol. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
QUICK FIX

— The House will vote on the farm bill this week, and the Supreme Court will hear arguments on a contentious pesticide labeling case.

— A USDA union invoked its right to bargain over the closure of day cares located in department buildings.

— A new Capitol area ad buy advocates blocking Proposition 12 through federal legislation.

IT’S MONDAY, APRIL 27. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips and pitches to rshin@politico.com and follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

THE MOMENT OF TRUTH: The House will vote on the farm bill Thursday, as Meredith reported over the weekend.

The legislation faces a narrow path forward as some Republicans, including Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.), threaten to oppose it unless its pesticide labeling language is removed. With the GOP’s slim majority, even a small cadre of Republicans could block the bill’s passage as most Democrats also plan to vote against it.

The provision, which would prevent pesticide makers from being sued over cancer warning labeling, is the biggest source of conflict surrounding the bill, as Grace and Meredith reported. However, other potential “yes” voters are also threatening to vote “no” over myriad issues.

President Donald Trump and many Republican lawmakers have said they feel urgency to pass the bill, which could sway rural voters in November’s midterm elections, especially as farm country struggles with the high costs of fertilizer and fuel stemming from the war in Iran.

Other big questions about the legislation’s final form loom ahead of Thursday, and the House Rules Committee will meet at 1 p.m. today to consider hundreds of amendments on issues including pesticides, food aid and the blocking of California’s Proposition 12.

Rep. Andrew Garbarino (R-N.Y.) told MA Sunday that his top request is a vote on an amendment to remove the “Save Our Bacon Act,” which would overturn Proposition 12, from the bill. He said he hasn’t gotten an indication of whether the Rules Committee or leaders will push for a vote on it.

He said he won’t oppose a procedural vote on the rule but that his vote on final passage will depend on how the bill changes during the Rules process.

“I know some of my colleagues are not happy with my stance — one of them told me I was breaking his heart,” Garbarino said, adding that he was concerned about how the bill would affect existing rules and regulations in New York.

“So I think we have to be very careful about the way all this all moves forward,” he said.

A bipartisan amendment introduced by Rep. Michelle Fischbach (R-Minn.) would allow the year-round sale of E15 and reform the Renewable Fuel Standard. The proposal had 20 co-sponsors, including House Rural Domestic Energy Council Co-Chairs Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa) and Stephanie Bice (R-Okla.).

While year-round E15 enjoys widespread bipartisan support among ag-state lawmakers, Ag Committee leaders have said the issue is not in its jurisdiction, so it would require a waiver from House leadership to be lumped into the farm bill. It is unclear whether Speaker Mike Johnson will grant the waiver.

Where the Dems stand: Two of the seven Democrats who voted to advance the farm bill out of committee, Reps. Josh Riley (D-N.Y.) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.) told MA that they plan to vote for it again on the floor. But Republicans will likely still have to count on centrist Democrats voting for the bill to have a chance at passage due to infighting over the contentious provisions.

Also on the Hill this week: The House Appropriations Committee will mark up the Ag-FDA budget for fiscal 2027 Tuesday. It is expected to run late into the night and could spill into Wednesday.
 

A message from Bayer:

86% of Americans think science misinformation is getting worse according to new data from a survey conducted by The Harris Poll on behalf of Bayer. When that misinformation targets modern farming practices, the fallout is real. Farmers face regulatory uncertainty while consumers grow more anxious about food safety. Still, a bipartisan majority of Americans agree; rigorous, evidence-based science is necessary for the country’s future. Dig into the numbers.
 
IN THE COURTS

ON THE DOCKET: The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments today for Monsanto v. Durnell, a case that has been at the center of the political battle over glyphosate, the active ingredient in the herbicide Roundup.

The case weighs whether Bayer, which acquired Monsanto in 2018, should be preempted from failure-to-warn claims for cancer risks associated with pesticide use.

It has been a political flash point between the Make America Healthy Again movement and the White House. The Trump administration filed a brief in December in support of the chemical company and released an executive order aiming to boost production of glyphosate earlier this year.

MAHA leaders are hosting a rally titled “The People vs. Poison” at 9 a.m. in front of the high court. Speakers will include MAHA advocates Vani Hari and Tony Lyons and Reps. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky.).
 

A message from Bayer:
 
AT THE AGENCIES

FIRST IN MA: The Department of Agriculture and one of its staff unions will begin facing off today over the department’s planned day care closures.

The USDA Child Development Center will cease operations this summer after the company running the facility declined to sign a new contract with the department, as your host first reported last week.

But Collin Bradley, president of AFSCME Local 3976, which represents staff at the Foreign Agricultural Service, said the union did not receive notice of the closures from the USDA itself, as required by its bargaining agreement.

KinderCare notified USDA parents that the day cares in the department’s Yates Building and the George Washington Carver Center would close on July 10, according to two KinderCare emails obtained by POLITICO.

“I think one of the things that has angered people so much is the complete lack of communication or care from the department level,” Bradley told MA. “It seems like they're not even telling their subagencies about it and they're just leaving employees in a lurch.”

Bradley said USDA has also not fulfilled a union contract child care provision related to the department’s sweeping reorganization plans.

“We have a specific language about if they move employees away from the South building, they have to do a survey of the employees, see what the child care needs are and then make changes based on those recommendations,” Bradley said. “That has not been done yet, even though it's been a year since they announced that they're moving people out.”

USDA announced in July 2025 that it would relocate much of its Washington-area staff to regional hubs across the country. Deputy Agriculture Secretary Stephen Vaden has said he expects employees will move to their reassigned locations this summer, coinciding with the day cares’ closure.

USDA spokesperson Alec Varsamis said in a statement that “the impending closure of the KinderCare facility in the Yates Building has nothing to do with the Department’s reorganization; as has been made clear, the Yates building will remain and continue to house USDA employees.”

Some USDA employees who use the day cares said the closures will mean added strain to their lives, longer commutes and possibly higher costs, as department employees pay a subsidized lower fee to enroll in the in-house child care.

Union representatives are scheduled to meet with USDA’s labor relations staff Monday afternoon to begin a bargaining process over the planned closure. Bradley said that because child care is an essential service, it is incumbent upon USDA to find another day care vendor for the space.
 

A message from Bayer:

Misinformation about agricultural science spreads faster than facts, creating uncertainty for farmers and policymakers alike. Yet here's what the data show: 88% of Republicans and 92% of Democrats agree rigorous science is necessary for progress. Americans haven't given up on evidence-based science - they're exhausted by viral misinformation and hungry for credibility.

A new survey conducted by The Harris Poll on behalf of Bayer on what Americans actually think about science and trust. The results reveal both challenge and opportunity - and shows policymakers that Americans value continued investment in research, innovation, and the scientific process.

See the findings for yourself and voice your support for science and the evidence-based outcomes it brings. Learn more.
 
Influence and Industry

MA EXCLUSIVE: The Center for the Environment and Welfare is rolling out an ad buy in the Washington, D.C., market this week in opposition to California’s Proposition 12, coinciding with the anticipated vote on the farm bill.

The commercial argues Proposition 12 has elevated grocery prices. It will air on CNN, MSNBC’s “Morning Joe,” and Fox News’ “Fox & Friends.”

“Farmers have to spend millions and millions of dollars to rebuild barns to be California compliant,” the ad says. “Those costs are passed on to consumers across America, even if they don't live in California, and low-income Americans are being hit hardest.”

“Congress is considering a fix that will help reduce your food costs and mix California's law before it gets worse,” it continues.

Dozens of House Democrats recently sent a letter to the chamber’s leadership opposing the provision, and it’s unclear whether it will remain in the final text amid opposition from some Republicans including Garbarino.
Row Crops

— Canada is launching a new forestry strategy as the sector continues to get walloped by the Trump administration’s trade war, our Zi-Ann Lum reports.

— First lady Melania Trump announced in a post on X the addition of a beehive housing two colonies to the White House honey program.

THAT’S ALL FOR MA! Drop us a line and send us your agriculture job announcements or events: gyarrow@politico.com, marciabrown@politico.com, rshin@politico.com, jperez@politico.com and gmott@politico.com.

item.title: SNAP and the farm bill’s fate
item.description: SNAP and the farm bill’s fate
item.content:encoded:
Presented by Growth Energy: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by Growth Energy

With help from Grace Yarrow

“I think we need to have a serious conversation about SNAP and, in particular, the way we calculate it,” said Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.). | Francis Chung/POLITICO
QUICK FIX

— Senate Ag Democrats want changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program’s cost-sharing model included in the chamber's farm bill.

— More than a dozen projects at the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center are set to be eliminated or have their funding reduced due to budget cuts, according to an audio recording of an all-hands meeting.

— Food aid groups expressed concern that reorganization of the Department of Agriculture’s nutrition program employees will interfere with the distribution of assistance.

IT’S MONDAY, MAY 4. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips to rshin@politico.com. Follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

TODAY: Jonathan Greenberger kicks off his first week as Global Editor-in-Chief for POLITICO. In a note shared with readers and subscribers, Greenberger spoke to how innovation has been part of POLITICO’s DNA from the start and emphasized continuing to evolve the ways we deliver our journalism. Read the full note here.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

A message from Growth Energy:

American farmers are speaking out: Year-round E15 is a win for everyone. It delivers lower-cost fuel for drivers, stronger markets for farmers, and greater U.S. energy security. Congress must act NOW to unlock affordable options at the pump.
 
DRIVING THE DAY

RENEWED DEMANDS: Several Senate Democrats said their support for the House’s version of the farm bill is contingent on changes to the cost-share framework for SNAP that were enacted last summer as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

“We need to have a bicameral negotiation between the House and the Senate on a bipartisan farm bill,” Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) told MA. “That negotiation has to include some sort of relief on the drastic cuts to SNAP. I hear about this as much from Republican county commissioners in Minnesota as from anyone because they're very worried about the big cost shifts that are involved.”

Senate Ag ranking member Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) said in a statement after the House passed its farm bill Thursday that committee Democrats are “committed to ensuring all states are treated equally by delaying the new SNAP cost shifts.”

The Republican megalaw requires states with SNAP error rates of 6 percent and above to split the financial burden of the program with the federal government. Some state officials have said the plan could leave them unable to afford to run the program at full capacity.

“I think we need to have a serious conversation about SNAP and, in particular, the way we calculate it,” said Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.). “I'm glad it's over here in the Senate and we can actually now get to it, even if we still have some big differences between us.”

Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) said the House legislation “did nothing to help states that are going to be devastated” by SNAP cuts.

The Senate faces a tight timeline for negotiating, passing and delivering a farm bill to President Donald Trump’s desk before Congress’ August recess. The path is further complicated by an array of other bills competing for the chamber’s attention ahead of midterm elections.

“We've got a couple of banking measures that could consume a lot of time, so you could just run out of runway, and we've got to prioritize,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said. “If I've got a choice between some of those issues and getting the NDAA and farm bill out, then I've got to favor NDAA and farm bill.”

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) said the year-round E15 bill that was decoupled from the farm bill is a higher priority for him than the farm bill.

“Year-round E15 is so much more important than what’s left of the farm bill. We passed the important things on the farm bill already,” Marshall told MA Thursday. “That’s my focus right now.”
 

A message from Growth Energy:
 
AROUND THE AGENCIES

FIRST IN MA: More than a dozen research projects underway at the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center will be terminated or receive reduced funding, Agricultural Research Service Administrator Joon Park said at an all-hands meeting, according to an audio recording obtained by MA.

The internal meeting came after USDA announced it would move most of its research and economics employees to regional hubs and start the process of decommissioning the research complex in Maryland.

BARC employees received emails last week about whether their research will continue to be funded and whether they will be relocated from the Washington area, according to two sources familiar and two versions of the notice previously obtained by MA.

Park said a “group of our colleagues at BARC received a notification stating that the FY26 congressional funding budget from Congress for this fiscal year terminated nine research projects at BARC, as well as reduced funding for eight research projects at BARC,” per the recording.

Employees working on those projects will receive a letter reassigning them to vacancies at ARS, Park added.

A USDA spokesperson told MA in a statement that for fiscal 2026, Congress reduced ARS funding for research in certain areas by over $32 million and increased spending for "higher priority" projects.

"For BARC, this resulted in the elimination of funding for 9 research projects and reduction of funding for 8 research projects across the areas of crop protection, livestock protection, and food safety," the spokesperson said in a statement. "The remaining funding and associated research for those 8 projects with reduced funding will be reassigned to other ARS locations."

More context: The House Appropriations Committee advanced a fiscal 2027 Agriculture-FDA funding bill last month that included a provision that would block USDA from using funds to close ARS facilities without prior notification to Congress.
 

A message from Growth Energy:

Across the country, farmers are calling on Congress to pass year-round E15. Made with homegrown energy, E15 lowers costs for American families, supports rural economies, and strengthens our nation’s energy security. Congress can act NOW to give consumers more choices at the pump while supporting U.S. agriculture. Discover why farmers across the country support year-round E15.
 
Food Security Outlook

REORG BACKLASH: Food aid groups slammed the Trump administration’s decision to move USDA’s Food and Nutrition Service employees across the country as part of the department’s sweeping reorganization plan, saying the move could worsen the operation of federal nutrition programs.

“These changes could undermine the close working relationships between State WIC Agencies and regional offices that are essential to day-to-day program operations,” Georgia Machell, president and CEO of the National WIC Association, said in a statement.

“It also offers no plan to retain experienced FNS staff or prevent the loss of institutional knowledge as employees are asked to relocate to new offices across the country,” Machell added.

FNS administers SNAP, the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children and free and reduced-cost school meals.

Thirty percent of FNS staff has already departed in the last year, in part due to offers of deferred resignation.

“I do not share their confidence that this reorg ‘will not disrupt program execution,’ especially since FNS is already so short-staffed,” Katie Bergh, senior policy analyst for food assistance at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said on X.
Row Crops

— Trump approved state permits for the 2026 red snapper recreational fishing season for Florida, Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina.

— The food industry sees a threat in Kennedy’s push to define “ultraprocessed” food. (The New York Times)

— Junk food is cheaper than healthful food, but a new study reinforces that taste preferences play a bigger role than prices. (The Washington Post Opinion)

THAT’S ALL FOR MA! Drop us a line and send us your agriculture job announcements or events: gyarrow@politico.com, marciabrown@politico.com, rshin@politico.com, jperez@politico.com and gmott@politico.com.

item.title: E15 dreams
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Grace Yarrow and Rachel Shin

An ethanol plant is pictured. | Scott Olson/Getty Images
QUICK FIX

— The clock is ticking for Congress to deliver on permanent year-round E15 promises.

— The United Nations’ international food price index rose for the third consecutive month.

— The Department of Agriculture issued a final rule to implement a law reinstating whole milk in school meals.

IT’S MONDAY, MAY 11. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! We're your hosts, Grace Yarrow and Rachel Shin. Send tips, pitches and exclusives to gyarrow@politico.com and rshin@politico.com. Follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

E15’S ‘BEST BET IN A WHILE’: The House is back in town this week with a familiar but politically potent demand hanging over it: deliver permanent, year-round access to E15.

Vulnerable Midwestern Republicans, farm industry groups and even President Donald Trump have endorsed and pushed for the plan as a boon for corn growers and consumers ahead of the midterm elections. But fierce opposition from oil state lawmakers who argue it will hurt refiners could lead to another fight that might tank the plan.

House leaders infuriated farm state Republicans last month when they agreed to remove the ethanol bill from consideration alongside the farm bill at the last minute amid outcry from oil state Republicans. It was the second time this year that an E15 deal had been punted.

This week, lawmakers are set to vote on a procedural motion that would formally decouple E15 from the farm bill. Then they would vote on the final passage of the E15 plan.

The expected vote could put Speaker Mike Johnson in the position of having to alienate part of his caucus and risk his standing in the House — especially after Trump put him on the hook for delivering on E15.

Vice President JD Vance was in Des Moines last week alongside Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, campaigning for Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) and touting Republicans’ work on E15.

“We’ve got a lot of Iowa farmers that would love to sell more E15 into the market, and we’re fighting every day to help them,” Vance said, noting that Nunn has been working on legislation on the matter. “We’re working on it every single day.”

Biofuels backers are warning it could be a make-or-break issue for Republicans in November, pointing to nearly 10 swing districts in the Midwest that could shift the balance of power in the House.

“Does [Johnson] really want to hold on to the gavel?” asked one biofuels lobbyist. “Because at this rate, he won't — not when he's rolling 20 Midwesterners who have been crystal clear that we need this.”

“Candidly, since we [postponed] it months ago, there was real danger that that was going to be indefinitely delayed,” Nunn told POLITICO last month. “You know where I stand on E15. I’m going to make sure it comes to the floor in the same way we just did the farm bill.”

As you’ll recall: Trump said during a trip to Clive, Iowa, in January that Congress was “very close” to getting a deal on E15, acknowledging its importance in the region.

“I will sign it without delay, OK? I hope you remember us for the midterms,” Trump said at the time.

Reality check: Even if GOP leaders are able to overcome the House’s divide on the issue, the proposal would face an uncertain future in the Senate.

“God only knows” what will happen if the E15 bill is sent to the Senate, said one agriculture lobbyist who was granted anonymity to discuss the negotiations candidly.

“We've expended a lot of resources and time and effort to get this done in the House,” the lobbyist added. “It's our best bet in a while. We'll deal with that problem [in the Senate] when it arrives.”

One Republican Senate staffer who works for an opponent of the plan said the House’s proposal is a “nonstarter.”

“It won’t pass in the Senate. I feel very confident about that,” the staffer said.
Cost of Living

EYEWATERING PRICES: International food prices climbed for the third consecutive month in April, hitting their highest mark in over three years, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization.

The FAO’s food price index rose 1.6 percent from its March level. Much of the increase was driven by a 5.9 percent hike in the vegetable oil index, which reached its highest level since July 2022.

The increase lines up with the war in Iran’s disruption of the fertilizer and energy supply chains.

“The input costs are starting to be transmitted to the commodity prices, but at a very low pace,” FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero said. “The major increase is happening on vegetable oils.”

The global meat price index also climbed to a record high, rising 1.2 percent from March and up 6.4 percent from April 2025. The FAO attributed high meat prices to limited slaughter-ready supply and ongoing efforts to rebuild herds.

Torero warned that strengthening safety net programs for both farmers and consumers will be crucial if global food supply chains continue to be strained.

“We need to accelerate and be prepared in terms of social protection programs in case food prices start to rise significantly,” Torero said. “In the medium term, the recommendation is to assure that farmers can survive because their margins are very small.”
AROUND THE AGENCIES

GOT MILK? USDA issued a final rule allowing schools to serve whole and 2 percent milk, implementing the Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act that Trump signed into law in January.

“President Trump promised to Make America Healthy Again, and restoring whole milk to schools is a major step toward delivering on that promise,” Rollins said in a statement Friday.

The final rule gives schools guidance on returning whole and 2 percent milk to schools that participate in the National School Lunch Program, reversing Obama-era restrictions that limited products with high levels of saturated fat.

It is part of a process to align school meal standards with the new Dietary Guidelines for Americans, according to the department’s announcement.
Row Crops

— It’s time for Trump’s B-Team, the agency understudies who may step into leadership voids, to have a moment. Read POLITICO’s analysis of agency deputies who could later enter the spotlight, including USDA’s Stephen Vaden.

—Sens. Steve Daines (R-Mont.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), and Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) held meetings in Beijing and discussed opening China’s markets to agriculture trade across beef, wheat, potatoes and other sectors.

— The Trump administration plan to reorganize food aid employees drew ire from federal workers. (The Washington Post)

— Consumers aren’t cutting back on fast food, even as other costs climb. (The New York Times)

THAT’S ALL FOR MA! Drop us a line and send us your agriculture job announcements or events: gyarrow@politico.com, marciabrown@politico.com, rshin@politico.com, jperez@politico.com and gmott@politico.com.
 

Follow us on X

item.title: The GOP’s food fight
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Grace Yarrow

With help from Marcia Brown

American consumers are only just beginning to feel the impact of a convergence of crises that are raising the cost of food at every step. | Erin Hooley/AP Photo
QUICK FIX

— The Iran war is forcing Republicans to confront the distressing reality that food prices likely won't drop before the midterm elections.

— The White House is weighing how to move forward with executive actions designed to bring down the cost of beef.

— President Donald Trump’s trip to Beijing produced new markets for U.S. meat and other ag products — though details are scarce.

IT'S MONDAY, MAY 18. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Grace Yarrow, filling in while my colleagues are out this week. Send tips, farm bill hot takes and other thoughts to gyarrow@politico.com. And, as always, follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

(GROCERY) BILLS, BILLS, BILLS: American consumers are only just beginning to feel the impact of a convergence of crises — prompted by war, weather and trade policy — that are raising the cost of food at every step, from fields to grocery shelves.

Consumer prices in April rose at their highest rate since May 2023, according to most recent inflation data, thanks largely to ballooning energy costs prompted by the shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz. A separate indicator that often previews inflation that will later hit consumers had its highest monthly gain in four years in April.

And the vise on consumer prices is tightening at the worst moment for Trump and the GOP as they campaign on economic stewardship ahead of November’s elections.

“If we're not really concerned about the midterms, then Republicans must be living in a cave,” Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) said of the impact of rising food prices.

How we got here: Fertilizer prices have skyrocketed, forcing farmers to reconsider how many acres they plant. Diesel fuel prices, which have shot to near-record levels since the war began, have made it more expensive to truck and refrigerate food. Even the cost of oil-based packaging like plastic has started to tick up.

Farmers are bracing for a super El Niño weather pattern that is expected to hammer crops with extreme rains and drought this year. And parched land in the West has already pushed ranchers to sell off much of their cattle, leading to record-high beef prices.

The Trump administration's tariffs have increased the price of critical supplies like aluminum — which is also affected by the closing of the strait — as well as some fresh produce, costs that parts of the food industry are already passing on to consumers, economists say.

"You have a perfect storm in this right now hitting food," said Jason Miller, a professor of supply chain management at Michigan State University.

Voters are already feeling the pain: Seventy-three percent of Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 say food prices have increased greatly or somewhat since the president took office, according to a new POLITICO Poll conducted by Public First from May 9-11. More than half of Americans ranked the cost of living as a top issue facing the United States.

Don’t miss the full story from Marcia here.

SPEAKING OF FOOD PRICES: The White House is deciding how to proceed with a potential executive order that officials hope will address a politically fraught domestic policy challenge that has vexed top aides for months: sky-high beef prices.

Trump planned last week to sign an executive order to ease tariffs on imported beef temporarily — a move that was delayed amid intense backlash from farm-state lawmakers and industry allies.

The executive order could help lower prices for consumers, though by how much remains uncertain. But doing so would drive up competition for American ranchers as they simultaneously face a host of higher costs brought on, in part, by the Iran war.

It’s not the first time Trump has been caught between pleasing ranchers, a loyal GOP constituency, and addressing affordability. But calls for consumer relief are growing as beef prices in the U.S. soar, rising another 2.7 percent, on average, just last month.

Ground beef — a staple of summer cookouts — is approaching $7 a pound, up roughly 12 percent from last summer.

“[Trump] owns hotels and country clubs. They buy beef. He’s acutely aware of it,” said a person close to the White House, who added that while there’s still hope the president can lower prices, there are fears relief won’t reach voters in time.

“You worry that people aren’t feeling it by the time Election Day rolls around,” said the person, granted anonymity to discuss the matter candidly.

Still, Republicans on the Hill are warning the administration that reducing tariffs on imported beef could hardly come at a worse time. Ranchers are already struggling with drought and the threat of the parasitic New World screwworm that could further shrink the country’s small herd — one of the root causes of high prices.

“I know that there were efforts, lobbying efforts, made to explain to the White House the challenges that creates for agriculture producers, presumably ranchers,” Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) said.

Don’t miss the full story from Myah Ward, your host and Daniel Desrochers.
EYE ON CHINA

MORE DETAILS? The White House announced China will purchase at least $17 billion of U.S. ag products per year for the next three years following Trump’s trip to Beijing last week.

Agriculture industry groups and Republican allies were anticipating the president could make progress on new trade agreements or solidify those negotiated last year.

The White House also touted that China restored market access for beef producers by renewing hundreds of expired export licenses, according to a fact sheet published Sunday. China also will resume imports of poultry from U.S. states that the Department of Agriculture has determined have no avian influenza.

Read more from POLITICO’s Ari Hawkins here.
AROUND THE AGENCIES

PERSONNEL MOVES: Aubrey Bettencourt, USDA’s top conservation official, told employees she was stepping down Friday, according to four people familiar with the news and an email obtained by MA.

Associate Chief Colton Buckley will “assume the role of Chief” of the Natural Resources Conservation Service effective today, according to the email Bettencourt sent to staff Friday. Buckley is a Turning Point USA alum and previously was CEO of the National Association of Resource Conservation and Development Councils.

“I could not be more confident in this decision, prouder of what we have accomplished, or more excited of what is to come for our Service,” Bettencourt wrote in the email.

Next up: Bettencourt is moving to a role at the Interior Department, according to two of the people familiar with the talks, who were granted anonymity to discuss the not-yet-public personnel change.

“I'm not going far — I will continue advocating for the farmers and ranchers we serve every day,” Bettencourt wrote.

Read the full scoop from Marcia and yours truly here.
On the Hill

FIRST IN MA: The Independent Beef Association of North Dakota is urging the Trump administration to investigate an “extraordinary” drop in the cattle futures market last October.

When Trump suggested in the fall that he would roughly double the tariff-free quota for Argentine beef, the futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange “collapsed and recovered for contracts that were due long before any increase in imported beef would occur,” the group wrote. They estimated cattle ranchers suffered losses of more than $104 million as a result.

“We ask that your agencies investigate whether market manipulation or other illegal acts caused prices to fall as much as they did,” they wrote.
Transitions

Brad Matsik will be the head of Wells Fargo’s new Food, Beverage and Agribusiness division.
Row Crops

— House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) and ranking member Angie Craig (D-Minn.) wrote a letter to Trump urging him to appoint a full panel of bipartisan commissioners to the Commodities Future Trading Commission.
